name: Тура попереду пішака
description:
We know from the previous lesson that we prefer to have the rook behind the passed pawn. However, there are situations in which the rook in front of the pawn can be successful. We ended the previous lesson with an example in which the passed pawn was one square away from promotion. There the defender was then able to keep a draw, but in this lesson we will see that there are also ways to do benefit from situations where the rook is in front of its own passed pawn.

In Example 1, white removes the rook in front of the pawn with check.

In Example 2, White removes the rook in front of the pawn and introduces a checkmate threat in the process.

In Example 3, white removes the rook in front of the pawn and thereby brings a trick into the position. If white captures the pawn, white has a skewer check.

In Example 4, we see that the lesson about simplification comes in handy. White removes the rook in front of the pawn, forcing the opponent to exchange rooks a move later. After that exchange, white reaches a winning pawn endgame.

What do you have to do?

Remove the rook in front of the pawn in such a way that you win material or obtain a winning endgame. In some situations you need a preparatory move first.

examples.text: With 1.Rg8+, white removes the rook in front of the pawn with check. This gives black no time to capture the pawn. After 1...Kf7 white promotes: 2.a8Q.

White brings a mate threat into the position with 1.Re8. After 1...Rxa7 2.e5# Black is mated. If White tries to avoid mate (for example by 1...g5) then White can promote (although more good moves are possible here).

In the previous examples, white removed the rook with a direct attack (check) or threat (mate). Here the rook's attack comes only after black captures the pawn.

With R.Th8 white lures the black rook to a7 where the piece is placed on the same row as the king (if black does not capture, white promotes): 1...Rxa7. Now white continues with 2.Rh7+ a skewer! 2...Kg6 3.Rxa7. White won a rook.

White can simplify into a pawn endgame with 1.Rd8. Here, the intermediate check 1...Ta6+ seems smart, but after 2.Kb7 Black has two problems: the rook is attacled and White threatens to promote on the next move. Black has to give their rook for the pawn.

After 1...Rxa7 2.Rd7+ Rxd7 3.Kxd7 it doesn't end well for black either. In the lesson 'conquering the pawn' you learned how to finish this with white. An example variation: 3...Kf7 4.Kd6 Kf8 5.Ke6 Kg7 6.Ke7 Kg8 7.Kxf6 Kf8 8.Ke6 Ke8 9.f6 Kf8 10.f7 Kg7 11.Ke7 Kg6 12.f8Q.

Simplifying with 1.Rc8 is also good. After 1...Rxa7 2.Rc7+ Rxc7 3.Kxc7 the pawn endgame is won for White.

texts: Try to clear the way for your pawn with check.
